1002.title: the Ashtavakra Gita complete
1002.hook: the king has just declared himself free, and the sage answers by asking why he still wants money
1002.howItsDone: Some readers of the Ashtavakra Gita take chapters two, three and four together: Janaka's declaration, the sage's testing questions, and Janaka's calm reply, as a model of how a teacher checks a student's realization.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ashtavakra Gita's second chapter: Janaka's cry of wonder, and the waves that turned out to be water. Did a wave come and go? Today, the teacher answers the cry. Day one thousand two.

What does a good teacher do when a student announces, I've got it? A whole chapter of joy has just poured out of King Janaka. Spotless, at peace, salutation to me. A different book might end right there, with the student shining and the teacher nodding. The Ashtavakra Gita doesn't. Chapter three opens with the sage leaning in, and his tone is almost dry. If you really know yourself as the one, imperishable Self, he asks, how is it that you're still keen on piling up wealth? It's a question aimed straight at a king, who has a treasury, and at anyone who has ever made a big announcement about themselves.
screen: `I'VE GOT IT.` → `THE TEACHER LEANS IN.` → `THEN WHY STILL PILE UP WEALTH?`

segments.voice: Much of the sage's third chapter is questions like that one, in paraphrase. You know the Self as one and imperishable. So why the hunger to get more? Then he gives a picture. Someone on a beach sees a glint in a shell, takes the mother-of-pearl for silver, and a little greed wakes up. The greed is real. The silver isn't. In the same way, he says, wanting for the world rises out of not knowing the Self. He goes on, and each question pokes at a different spot: desire, attachment, the pull of pleasure. Isn't it strange, he keeps asking, that one who knows so much still reaches like this? Some readers find the chapter harsh, especially after the joy of the one before. On one reading, the test protects the student. Words like spotless and at peace are easy to say. The test is whether the hand still closes around the silver. Ashtavakra isn't calling Janaka a liar. He's asking him to check whether the knowing has reached his habits yet, or only his mouth. And in the next chapter Janaka answers, calmly. The one who knows the Self, he says, can move through the world as though it were a game, not weighed down by it. He doesn't take back what he said. He shows the sage where he stands. That's the shape these two chapters make together. A claim, a test, and an answer to the test. The wonder of chapter two isn't canceled by chapter three. It's checked, and checking is part of how this book takes knowledge seriously.
screen: `THE TEACHER ANSWERS WONDER WITH A TEST.` · `SILVER IN A SHELL.` · `HAS IT REACHED THE HABITS, OR ONLY THE MOUTH?` · `JANAKA ANSWERS: LIFE AS A GAME.` · then, large: `A CLAIM, A TEST, AN ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one thing you've been reaching for lately: a purchase, a bit of praise, a result. Don't judge the reaching. Just look at it the way the sage looks at Janaka. Is it silver, or a glint in a shell? Notice where the wanting sits in the body, the chest, the jaw, the hands. Breathe into that place, and let the hand open a little. The bell holds the time.
The Ashtavakra Gita, chapter three: the sage tests the king's wonder by asking why he still reaches, like someone taking a shell for silver.
Your line: the Ashtavakra Gita, complete. Today, before one thing you reach for, a cart, a scroll, a second helping, ask the sage's question: silver, or a shell? Day one thousand two.

1003.title: the Ashtavakra Gita complete
1003.hook: a teaching book tells its reader that all the reading won't settle them until they forget it all
1003.howItsDone: Some teachers of the Ashtavakra Gita explain its praise of idleness as the end of inner striving rather than of outward work, and its call to forget everything as letting go of holding the teaching itself as a possession.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ashtavakra Gita's test: the sage asking the king why he still reached for silver that was only a shell. Did you catch a shell? Day one thousand three.

Somewhere on a shelf there's a stack of books about letting go, and every one of them is something else to hold on to. The Ashtavakra Gita seems to know that joke. Deep in the book, the sage turns to the student, and to anyone reading over his shoulder, and says something that could make a diligent reader put the page down. You can talk about the scriptures and listen to them, my child, as much as you like. But you won't rest in yourself until you forget it all. It's a book telling its reader that the reading isn't the point. And a few verses later, it praises someone the sage calls a master of idleness.
screen: `BOOKS ABOUT LETTING GO.` → `FORGET IT ALL.` → `A MASTER OF IDLENESS.`

segments.voice: This is chapter sixteen, in paraphrase. First the line about forgetting. Then the sage goes on. You may enjoy, you may work, you may meditate, he says, but the mind will still long for what lies beyond all of that, where wanting goes quiet. Then a sentence that sounds almost like a diagnosis. Everyone is unhappy because of their striving, and nobody notices. And then a verse that can sound like a joke. Happy, the sage says, is the great idler, the one for whom even opening and closing the eyes is a bother. No one else. Read straight, that sounds like a blessing on the couch. The verses around it point another way. Every one of them is about effort of a particular kind: the strain of the one who thinks I am the doer, the pushing and grasping we met a few days ago as a black snake. The master idler isn't someone who won't wash the dishes. It's someone in whom that inner straining has stopped. The dishes may still get washed. Nobody inside is clenching about it. Teachers often read the forgetting the same way. On that reading, the sage isn't asking Janaka to forget his kindness or his duties. He's asking him to stop holding the teaching like a possession, a set of correct ideas to defend. Knowledge that's carried around like luggage is still something extra to carry. This chapter is the book turning on itself, gently. It has spent pages pointing at freedom, and now it says the pointing has to drop away too. The Vivekachudamani gave a warning like it, about clever talk of scripture, and here the Ashtavakra Gita gives it its own way.
screen: `FORGET IT ALL.` · `UNHAPPY BECAUSE OF STRIVING.` · `THE GREAT IDLER: NO INNER STRAINING.` · `DON'T CARRY THE TEACHING LIKE LUGGAGE.` · then, large: `THE POINTING DROPS AWAY TOO.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and, for these two minutes, try the sage's kind of idleness. Don't manage the breath. Don't follow a technique. Don't try to remember anything from this week, not even today's lesson. If you notice yourself trying to sit well, let that go too. Whatever is here, let it be here without doing anything about it. If the eyes want to close, let them, and if they want to open, let them. The bell holds the time.
The Ashtavakra Gita, chapter sixteen: forget it all, and the great idler, in whom the inner straining has stopped.
Your line: the Ashtavakra Gita, complete. Today, during one ordinary chore, do it fully, and see if you can let the one inside who clenches about it take the afternoon off. Day one thousand three.

1004.title: the Ashtavakra Gita complete
1004.hook: the last chapter is one small word asked over and over: where?
1004.howItsDone: The Ashtavakra Gita ends with Janaka's chapter of questions beginning with kva, where; some students reread it slowly at the close of their study, asking each where for themselves.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ashtavakra Gita told us to forget it all, and praised the great idler, in whom the straining stops. Did a chore get done without the clenching? Today, the last chapter, and the end of a long stretch of the path. Day one thousand four.
screen: `THE ASHTAVAKRA GITA.` · `FORGET IT ALL.` · `TODAY: THE LAST CHAPTER.`

segments.voice: Kva. In Sanskrit it means where. It's a small word, the kind a child uses looking for a lost shoe. And the last chapter of the Ashtavakra Gita is built almost entirely out of it. Janaka speaks, and verse after verse he asks where. Not where is my kingdom, or where did I leave the keys. He asks where things are that this path spends so long seeking. By the end of the chapter, the word has asked about nearly everything, and the book simply stops.
screen: `KVA: WHERE.` → `VERSE AFTER VERSE.` → `THEN THE BOOK STOPS.`

segments.voice: Here's the shape of it, in paraphrase. Where are the elements, Janaka asks, where is the body, where are the senses, where is the mind, for me, spotless by nature? Where is scripture? Where is knowledge of the Self? And then, the line that stops a reader short. Where is bondage, and where is liberation? A verse later he even asks: where is the karma already begun, where is freedom while living? Those are the very ideas the Vivekachudamani ended on. Bondage and liberation, those two words have carried this whole book. Janaka asked about freedom on the first page. The sage told him he was free if he took himself as free. Now, at the end, the student isn't celebrating his freedom. He's saying that for what he is, even the words bound and free have nowhere to stand. That's why this is a where and not a no. He isn't arguing that scripture is wrong or that liberation is a myth. He's looking for them in awareness itself, and finding nothing there that needs them. On this reading, the medicine has done its work, and the bottle can go back on the shelf. That's the Ashtavakra Gita, complete, in large steps. A king asks how to be free. A sage tells him he already is. The king cries out in wonder. The sage tests him. The book tells him to forget even the book. And the king's last word is where. It also closes the lineage track for this year, three roads in turn. Karma: the Gita's chapters on action, and a year of service designed. Bhakti, the Gita Govinda, the Bhagavata's tenth book and the kirtan songs. And jnana, the Vivekachudamani and this book. Three roads, each with its own voice, and none asked to stand in for the others. Tomorrow the path turns to practice again, starting with the breath.
screen: `WHERE IS THE BODY, THE MIND, SCRIPTURE?` · `WHERE IS BONDAGE? WHERE IS LIBERATION?` · `A WHERE, NOT A NO.` · `THE BOOK IN SIX STEPS.` · then, large: `KARMA, BHAKTI, JNANA.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Then borrow Janaka's small word. Where is the body? Notice it, and notice it appearing in awareness. Where is the mind? Notice a thought arise and pass. Where is the one who is trying to be free? Ask gently, without hunting for an answer. Each time a where comes up, let it open into the quiet that's left after the question. The bell holds the time.
The Ashtavakra Gita, complete: from a king's question about freedom to his last word, where, asked even of bondage and liberation.
Your line: the Ashtavakra Gita, complete. Today, when a worry insists it's everything, ask it the king's question, where are you, and watch what's left. Day one thousand four.

1005.title: pranayama sequences
1005.hook: in an Upanishad the body's powers argue over who holds it up, until the breath gets up to leave
1005.howItsDone: Pranayama is traditionally learned from a teacher; in many lineages a session begins sitting upright after some posture work, starting with gentle breath awareness and slow exhalation before any breath retention, and stopping at any dizziness or strain.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ashtavakra Gita, complete, ended with one word, where, and the lineage track closed: karma, bhakti, jnana. Did a worry go quiet when you asked it where? Today, a new stretch: practices, deeper. Day one thousand five.

The powers of the body are having an argument. Speech says it holds the body up. The eye says no, it does. The ear, the mind, the elements themselves all make the same boast. It's a scene from the Prashna Upanishad, told by a teacher named Pippalada to a student who has asked which powers keep a living being going. And in the middle of the shouting, one power speaks a single warning and then stops arguing. The breath. Prana. Nobody believes it, so it simply gets up, as if to leave.
screen: `THE BODY'S POWERS ARGUE.` → `EACH ONE BOASTS.` → `THE BREATH GETS UP TO LEAVE.`

segments.voice: Here's what happens next, in paraphrase. Prana, the chief power, has warned them: don't be fooled, I'm the one holding this body together. They don't believe it. So prana rises to go. And as it rises, every other power is pulled up with it, helpless to stay. When prana settles back down, they all settle. The Upanishad gives a picture: like bees that rise when the king bee rises, and settle when it settles. The argument is over. Speech, mind, eye and ear turn to prana and praise it. That little story sits under this whole week. Pranayama is the name for practices that work with prana by way of the breath. If the breath is what everything else rises and settles with, then working with the breath is a way of working with everything else too: the restless mind, the racing heart, the scattered attention. Over the next days we'll take these practices as sequences, one step set after another in an order, gentle ones before stronger ones. Two warnings belong right at the start. Breath practice is done gently. Nothing is forced, and nothing is held until it hurts. If there's dizziness or strain, stop and breathe normally. And anyone with a heart or lung condition, or who is pregnant, talks to a doctor before trying the stronger practices. Today there's nothing strong at all. Just the king bee, rising and settling, and everything else going with it.
screen: `PRANA RISES; EVERYTHING RISES.` · `LIKE BEES WITH THE KING BEE.` · `PRANAYAMA: WORKING WITH PRANA.` · `A SEQUENCE: ONE STEP AFTER ANOTHER.` · then, large: `GENTLY. NOTHING FORCED.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, spine easy, hands resting. Don't change the breath yet. Just watch it rise and settle, the way the bees follow the king bee. Notice what goes with it: the belly, the ribs, the shoulders, even the thoughts. Each in-breath, things lift a little. Each out-breath, they settle. After a while, let the out-breath become just a little slower than before, still easy. If anything strains, let it go back to normal. The bell holds the time.
Pranayama sequences: breath practices set in an order, working with prana, the power the others rise and settle with.
Your line: pranayama sequences. Today, when the mind is racing, notice one out-breath settling, and watch whether anything settles with it. Day one thousand five.

1006.title: pranayama sequences
1006.hook: in the Yoga Sutra the breath doesn't come first: it waits its turn, after the seat
1006.howItsDone: Where pranayama is taught in this order, it follows posture work: practitioners settle into a steady seat, move through gentle breath practices in a set order, and finish by resting in stillness or meditation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pranayama sequences began with an Upanishad: the breath rose, and every other power rose with it, like bees with the king bee. Did anything settle with an out-breath? Day one thousand six.
screen: `PRANAYAMA SEQUENCES.` · `LIKE BEES WITH THE KING BEE.`

segments.voice: In the Yoga Sutra of Patanjali, the path comes as a list of eight limbs, in order. Restraints. Observances. The seat. Then, fourth in line, pranayama. Then drawing the senses in. Then concentration, meditation, absorption. Someone looking for breathwork might be surprised to find it isn't first. It waits its turn. Before it come the ways a person treats others and treats themselves, and the seat, the steady posture. And after it, the senses drawn in and the mind gathered. The order is already a sequence, before anyone has counted a single breath.
screen: `EIGHT LIMBS, IN ORDER.` → `PRANAYAMA IS FOURTH.` → `THE BREATH WAITS ITS TURN.`

segments.voice: Here's how the sutras build it, in paraphrase. First, the seat. Posture, the text says, should be steady and easy. Not a feat. A way of sitting that can be held without fuss. Then, the sutra says, once the seat is in place, comes pranayama: a pause, a breaking, in the flow of the in-breath and the out-breath. The breath stops running on its own like a tap left open, and comes under gentle attention. Then the sutras say what that does. Through it, a covering over the inner light grows thin. And the mind becomes fit for concentration. Then comes the next limb, pratyahara, the senses drawn in. That's a sequence in the plainest sense. Each step makes the next one possible. A steady seat lets the breath settle. A settled breath lets the mind gather. A gathered mind can turn inward. Try to skip one and the next step wobbles. Trying to slow the breath while the knee aches and the back slumps is hard work. Trying to concentrate while the breath is ragged is harder. So a pranayama sequence built on this frame starts before the breath. It starts with how a person sits. Then it moves through breath practices in an order, gentle ones first. And it ends by handing over to stillness, not by stopping cold. The sutra doesn't give those exercises one by one; later manuals do. What it gives is the frame: seat, breath, senses, mind, each laid on the last like stones in a path.
screen: `FIRST: A SEAT, STEADY AND EASY.` · `THEN: A PAUSE IN THE FLOW OF BREATH.` · `THE MIND BECOMES FIT TO CONCENTRATE.` · `EACH STEP MAKES THE NEXT POSSIBLE.` · then, large: `SEAT, BREATH, SENSES, MIND.`

segments.voice: Let's string three short steps together, the sutra's way. First, the seat. Shift until the sitting feels steady and easy, nothing to fight. Then the breath. Let a few breaths go by, then let each out-breath slow a little, and notice the small pause at the bottom of it, without holding. Nothing forced. Then hand over. Let the breath go back to its own pace, and rest attention on one place, the touch of air at the nostrils. If any step wobbles, go back one. The bell holds the time.
Pranayama sequences: breath practice in an order, starting from a steady seat and ending in a mind gathered enough to turn inward.

Your line: pranayama sequences. Today, string two things together on purpose: settle how you're sitting first, then take three slow out-breaths, and notice whether the second step comes easier. Day one thousand six.

1007.title: pranayama sequences
1007.hook: in the middle of a list of offerings, the Gita slips in the breath itself
1007.howItsDone: Some Hindus who practice pranayama understand it, with Gita 4.29, as an offering in itself, and move through their breath practices in a set order, each one following on from the last.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pranayama sequences again: breath practices set one after another, in an order. When you strung two of them together, which one did the second build on? Day one thousand seven.

Chapter four of the Bhagavad Gita, and Krishna is making a list. Some people, he says, offer their sacrifice in fire. Some offer their wealth. Some offer study, some offer strict vows. It reads like a tour of the ways a person can give something up. And then, tucked into the list, a line that sounds almost like a breathing class. Some offer the in-breath into the out-breath, and the out-breath into the in-breath. No altar, no grain, no butter poured on flames. Just the breath, handed back and forth. Today, that one line, and what it does to the idea of a sequence.
screen: `THE GITA MAKES A LIST.` → `FIRE, WEALTH, STUDY, VOWS.` → `AND THEN: THE BREATH.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, in paraphrase. Gita chapter four, verse twenty-nine: some offer the in-breath into the out-breath, and the out-breath into the in-breath, checking the movement of both, devoted to the regulation of breath. That last phrase uses the word you've been carrying since the Prashna Upanishad two days ago. Pranayama is right there in the Sanskrit. Notice the shape of it. It's a sequence already, the simplest one there is: in, then out, then in. But the verse doesn't describe it as two things. It describes each half as an offering into the other. The out-breath isn't the end of something. It's what the in-breath is given to. And the in-breath is what the out-breath is given to. Around this verse, the chapter keeps widening what counts as sacrifice. A few verses later Krishna says that sacrifice made of knowledge is greater than sacrifice made of things. So a breath practice in this list isn't a warm-up before the real offering. It is one. That changes how a sequence feels from the inside. When you move from a slow count to a gentle pause to a humming breath, you can treat each step as finishing the last one, rather than replacing it. Nothing gets discarded. The quiet from the slow breath is handed to the pause. The pause is handed to the hum. Commentators read this verse in different ways. Some take it as a technical note about holding the breath between in and out. Others read it more widely, as one more inner offering in a chapter full of them. The text itself leaves room for both, and it doesn't stop to settle the question. What it does settle is that the breath belongs on the list.
screen: `IN-BREATH OFFERED INTO OUT-BREATH.` · `THE WORD PRANAYAMA IS IN THE VERSE.` · `BREATH COUNTS AS A SACRIFICE.` · `EACH STEP HANDED TO THE NEXT.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, spine easy. For a few breaths, change nothing. Just notice where the out-breath ends. Then, as the next breath comes in, let it feel like it's receiving what the last one let go. Now watch the two turning points: the moment the out-breath becomes the in-breath, and the moment the in-breath becomes the out-breath. Don't lengthen or hold anything. Just notice each turn, a handful of rounds. Then let go of watching, and let the breath carry on by itself. Three short steps, each handed to the next. If you pray, you can hold the Gita's picture lightly in mind: breath given into breath. The bell holds the time.
Pranayama sequences. Breath practices set in an order. Today, the Gita's picture of one: in-breath offered into out-breath, and back.
Your line: pranayama sequences. Today, once when you finish one task and start another, take a single slow breath between them and let the first one hand off to the second. Day one thousand seven.

1008.title: pranayama sequences
1008.hook: a hatha yoga manual compares the breath to a lion, an elephant and a tiger
1008.howItsDone: In some hatha yoga lineages, breath practices are learned in order, gentle ones first, with longer holds left until later and sometimes taught one to one by a teacher who watches the student.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pranayama sequences as offering: the in-breath given into the out-breath, each step handed to the next. Did one task hand off to another for you? Day one thousand eight.

A lion, an elephant and a tiger. Not the usual cast for a breathing lesson. But they turn up in the second chapter of the Hatha Yoga Pradipika, a manual for yogis, right where it starts teaching breath. Nobody walks up to a wild lion on the first day and puts a hand on its head. Taming one goes slowly, a little closer each day, until the animal can be handled. The text says the breath is like that. And then it adds a warning that is not gentle at all. Today, the order a sequence is built in, and why the old manual cared so much about going slowly.
screen: `A LION, AN ELEPHANT, A TIGER.` → `TAMED A LITTLE AT A TIME.` → `THE BREATH IS LIKE THAT.`

segments.voice: Here's the passage, in paraphrase. Chapter two, verse fifteen: as a lion, an elephant or a tiger is brought under control slowly, little by little, so the breath is brought under control. Otherwise, it harms the one who practices. The next verse adds that breath practice done properly helps, and done wrongly brings illness. That's striking from a book that loves breath practice. It isn't warning people off. It's warning them about order. Teachers have a Sanskrit word for this idea, though the verse doesn't use it: krama, a step, a sequence, going in order. A sequence isn't only a list of practices. It's a decision about what comes first and what has to wait. A few verses earlier the same chapter gives the reason breath matters at all: when the breath moves unsteadily, the mind is unsteady, and when the breath is still, the mind is still. So the breath is a way in to the mind. That's why the manual treats it with respect, the way a keeper treats a big animal. In practice, some teachers in the hatha tradition begin with the plain and the gentle, slow breathing and simple counting, and leave the long holds for later, sometimes learned one to one with someone watching. This week has followed that line: the breath as the power the others rise with, the seat before the breath, breath offered into breath, and today, the pace. And it's the end of a week that began with the Ashtavakra Gita, a text about the self that is already free and doesn't need to get anywhere. The two pull in different directions. The Ashtavakra Gita can sound impatient with practice; at one point the sage tells Janaka that practicing meditation is itself his bondage. The hatha manual is practice from start to finish. The tradition has kept both books, and some teachers read both.
screen: `TAMED LITTLE BY LITTLE.` · `DONE WRONGLY, IT HARMS.` · `UNSTEADY BREATH, UNSTEADY MIND.` · `GENTLE FIRST, LONG HOLDS LATER.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Begin with no technique at all, just a few breaths as they come. Then start a gentle count: in for four, out for four. When that's easy, stretch only the out-breath a little: in for four, out for five or six. Stay there. If anything strains, the chest, the throat, the jaw, return to the even count. That return is part of the sequence, not a failure of it. Near the end, drop the counting and let the breath settle by itself. The bell holds the time.
Pranayama sequences. Breath practices set in an order. Today, the pace of that order: little by little, the way a keeper tames a lion.
Your line: pranayama sequences. Today, pick one thing you're tempted to rush, and do only its first step properly before moving on. Day one thousand eight.

match.prompt: the lion and the breath — tap the pairs.
pairs: a step, an order, a sequence

myth: the Hatha Yoga Pradipika says breath practice is risk-free
it warns that breath forced too fast can harm, the way an untamed animal can.
the same chapter links a still breath with a still mind
it says when the breath moves unsteadily the mind is unsteady, and when the breath is still the mind is still.
going back a step in a sequence means the practice failed
in the manual's picture, slow progress is the method, not a setback.

fork.setup: you're new to breath practice and you've read about long breath holds. where do you start?
options: with the longest hold you can manage.
with gentle, slow breathing, holds left for later.
with whatever looks hardest, to save time.
fork.reveal: the Hatha Yoga Pradipika compares the breath to a lion tamed little by little, and warns that rushing it harms.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: krama, a step, a going in order; the idea behind any sequence.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pranayama sequence is a list of breathing exercises.
what it means: it's an order, gentle first and harder later, built slowly like taming an animal.
what a scholar hears: Hatha Yoga Pradipika 2.15–2.16 on gradual control of the breath, after 2.2 links unsteady breath with an unsteady mind.
